items.title: The Tolerant Chain
items.question: A paint strip changes imperceptibly from red to orange. If every adjacent pair must receive the same color label because their difference is tiny, then transitivity forces the two visibly different endpoints to receive the same label.
items.correctExplanation: True. Local tolerance plus transitivity propagates one label across the entire chain, producing the sorites conflict at the endpoints.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Each tiny step preserves the label under the tolerance premise; chaining all those equivalences makes the distant endpoints match even though the setup says they plainly differ.
items.lessonContent:
Sorites reasoning combines plausible local tolerance with repeated inference across a long series.
Transitivity can turn negligible pairwise differences into an implausible global verdict.
The contradiction pressures the tolerance rule, endpoint judgments, or classical inference.
Continuous transitions make the hidden cost of repeated categorization visible.
Share this: inspect a gradient today and ask which adjacent step supposedly changes its label.

items.title: Induction Misfires
items.question: If a predicate such as 'young' applies at age 20 and changing age by one day never changes its application, mathematical induction validly proves that every possible age is young.
items.correctExplanation: False. Induction would be valid only if the universal one-day preservation premise were true; vagueness makes that tolerance premise tempting, not guaranteed.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Mathematical induction faithfully transmits a genuine step rule, but the sorites problem is precisely whether 'one day can never matter' holds without exception across the whole range.
items.lessonContent:
Induction requires both a base case and a universally valid successor step.
Formal validity cannot rescue a plausible but false or unstable premise.
Vague predicates tempt us to promote local similarity into exceptionless preservation.
Audit the induction step rather than blaming the inference rule that uses it.
Share this: when someone says 'one more cannot matter,' ask whether that remains true at every stage.

items.title: The Hidden Cutoff
items.question: Epistemicism about vagueness can consistently claim that one exact millisecond separates 'soon' from 'not soon' even though speakers could never discover which millisecond it is.
items.correctExplanation: True. Epistemicism preserves a sharp extension while treating its boundary as unknowable because linguistic use cannot reveal it precisely.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The view distinguishes metaphysical sharpness from epistemic access: there is a last qualifying instant, but no feasible evidence tells speakers where it lies.
items.lessonContent:
Epistemicism treats vague predicates as sharply divided despite our ignorance of the divide.
Unknown boundaries need not be nonexistent boundaries on this account.
The view preserves classical truth values at the cost of radical semantic ignorance.
Its central challenge is explaining why the cutoff is both real and systematically inaccessible.
Share this: separate 'there is no fact' from 'we cannot know the fact' in one uncertain claim.

items.title: Either Side
items.question: Under supervaluationism, a borderline coat may be neither definitely blue nor definitely not blue, while 'the coat is blue or it is not blue' remains true on every admissible sharpening.
items.correctExplanation: True. Different precisifications may disagree on the coat, yet each classical precisification makes the disjunction true, so it is supertrue.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Supervaluationism permits truth-value gaps for borderline atomic claims while preserving some classical compounds that hold under every acceptable way of drawing the boundary.
items.lessonContent:
Supervaluationism evaluates vague language across multiple admissible precisifications.
A claim is supertrue when every acceptable sharpening makes it true.
Borderline atomic claims may lack a settled value even when classical tautologies survive.
This separates determinacy of parts from validity of a compound.
Share this: list two reasonable cutoffs for one vague category and test a disjunction under both.

items.title: Confidence or Degree
items.question: In fuzzy logic, assigning 0.7 truth to 'the room is warm' necessarily means there is a 70% chance that the room is fully warm and a 30% chance it is not warm at all.
items.correctExplanation: False. A fuzzy degree represents graded membership or truth, whereas probability represents uncertainty about which state obtains.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Seventy-percent warm can model partial satisfaction of a predicate even with complete information; a 70% probability instead measures uncertainty over alternatives.
items.lessonContent:
Degrees of truth and degrees of belief answer different questions.
Fuzzy logic models partial category membership along a graded scale.
Probability models uncertainty about facts or outcomes.
The numbers may look identical while carrying different logical roles.
Share this: label one percentage today as either uncertainty or degree before interpreting it.

items.title: Standards on Court
items.question: A 190-centimeter person can count as tall among all adults but not tall among professional basketball centers without contradiction, because contextualism lets the comparison standard shift.
items.correctExplanation: True. The predicate's threshold is supplied partly by the conversational comparison class, so the two utterances evaluate against different standards.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The person's height stays fixed, but 'tall' can select different thresholds in ordinary-adult and elite-center contexts; no single proposition is both affirmed and denied.
items.lessonContent:
Context-sensitive predicates draw standards from a comparison class or practical purpose.
Changing context can change content without changing the underlying object.
Apparent contradictions may disappear once hidden standards are made explicit.
Contextualism explains flexible use but must still constrain which shifts are legitimate.
Share this: add an explicit comparison class to one use of 'large,' 'fast,' or 'expensive' today.

items.title: A Line by Decree
items.question: A city defines 'high-rise' for taxes as any building at least 35 meters tall. This legal precisification proves that ordinary 'high-rise' had a naturally sharp 35-meter boundary all along.
items.correctExplanation: False. The city creates an operational boundary for a purpose; it does not discover a pre-existing semantic joint in ordinary usage.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Administrative precision can make decisions consistent while leaving the original predicate vague; stipulating a cutoff is not evidence that common language secretly contained it.
items.lessonContent:
Operational definitions replace a vague standard with a decision-ready rule.
Stipulated boundaries serve coordination without claiming metaphysical discovery.
Precision for one purpose may be inappropriate for another.
Confusing a useful map with a natural boundary turns convention into fact.
Share this: identify one cutoff in a policy and ask what practical purpose selected it.

items.title: Blur Around Blur
items.question: If cases are divided into clearly tall, borderline tall, and clearly not tall, the boundaries between 'clear' and 'borderline' may themselves be vague; adding one middle category does not necessarily end the regress.
items.correctExplanation: True. Higher-order vagueness appears when determinacy classifications inherit borderline cases of their own.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. A three-zone picture relocates the boundary problem unless it can sharply determine where clear cases stop and borderline ones begin.
items.lessonContent:
Higher-order vagueness concerns uncertainty in the boundary of the borderline region itself.
Adding labels can move rather than solve a classification problem.
Sharp meta-categories require justification just as first-order categories do.
The regress pressures theories that explain vagueness with one crisp middle zone.
Share this: when adding an 'uncertain' bucket, ask how its own edges will be assigned.

items.title: Two Meanings Apart
items.question: The word 'bank' is vague because riverbanks and financial banks are borderline instances of one gradually changing concept.
items.correctExplanation: False. That is lexical ambiguity between distinct meanings, not a borderline case along one meaning's extension.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Context selects between two established senses of 'bank'; vagueness instead persists after the intended sense is fixed because some cases resist classification.
items.lessonContent:
Ambiguity offers multiple meanings, while vagueness leaves borderline cases within one meaning.
Context can disambiguate a word yet leave its selected predicate vague.
Different diagnoses demand different repairs: choose a sense or sharpen a boundary.
Conflating the two obscures whether the problem is selection or classification.
Share this: take one unclear sentence and ask whether it has two readings or one fuzzy reading.

items.title: Sharper Comparison
items.question: Even if neither of two trees has a determinate verdict for 'tall,' the claim that one tree is taller than the other can be exact when their measured heights differ.
items.correctExplanation: True. The comparative can track an ordered measurement directly even when the positive adjective requires a vague contextual threshold.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Determining which height is greater does not require deciding where 'tall' begins, so comparative precision can coexist with categorical vagueness.
items.lessonContent:
Comparatives can order cases without dividing them into a positive category and its complement.
Measurements support exact greater-than relations even when labels need thresholds.
Replacing a vague absolute with a comparative often preserves the information actually needed.
Not all expressions built from a vague adjective inherit the same indeterminacy.
Share this: replace one vague rating today with a direct comparison between two options.

items.title: The Continuum Leap
items.question: Because no precise instant marks when dusk becomes night, it follows that there is no defensible difference between broad daylight and midnight darkness.
items.correctExplanation: False. A missing sharp boundary does not erase clear cases at distant parts of a continuum.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. The continuum fallacy wrongly infers that if adjacent or borderline stages resist separation, the endpoints cannot differ; vague categories can retain obvious central cases.
items.lessonContent:
The continuum fallacy treats absence of a sharp cutoff as absence of any distinction.
Clear positive and negative cases can surround an indeterminate middle.
Gradual change does not make distant endpoints equivalent.
Reasoning on spectra requires tolerating uncertain boundaries without flattening the scale.
Share this: answer one 'where exactly?' challenge by naming clear cases on both ends first.

items.title: One Drop Added
items.question: Starting with a clearly dry sponge and adding water drop by drop yields a reverse sorites: if one drop can never turn a non-wet sponge wet, repeated reasoning says the soaked endpoint is still non-wet.
items.correctExplanation: True. Sorites chains work in the additive direction as well as the subtractive direction; the questionable tolerance step propagates the starting label.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The endpoint is plainly soaked, but universal one-drop preservation carries 'non-wet' through every stage, exposing the same local-to-global conflict in reverse.
items.lessonContent:
Sorites sequences can add tiny increments or remove them.
Direction does not matter when a tolerance premise preserves a label at each adjacent step.
Both forms expose tension between clear endpoints and locally indistinguishable transitions.
Testing a chain in reverse can reveal assumptions hidden by a familiar presentation.
Share this: reverse one gradual-change argument and see whether its premise remains plausible.

items.title: Risk Along the Slope
items.question: A sorites argument about vague boundaries and a slippery-slope argument about a chain of future causes are logically identical, because both mention many small steps.
items.correctExplanation: False. Sorites concerns repeated preservation of a vague predicate, while a slippery slope predicts causal or normative escalation between events.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Shared stepwise imagery does not make the inferences identical: one pressures classification boundaries, while the other needs evidence that each event will trigger the next.
items.lessonContent:
Similar narrative shapes can hide different inferential mechanisms.
Sorites chains preserve a predicate across neighboring cases.
Slippery slopes forecast causal, institutional, or normative transitions.
The right audit asks whether each link is semantic tolerance or empirical causation.
Share this: label each link in one stepwise warning as a definition, cause, or value judgment.

items.title: Precision Without Truth
items.question: Measuring every hair on a person's head with perfect accuracy would by itself settle whether the person is bald, because all vagueness is caused by imperfect observation.
items.correctExplanation: False. Exact data can remove measurement uncertainty while leaving the predicate's application boundary unsettled.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Knowing the exact count answers an empirical question, but 'bald' may still lack an agreed or determinate threshold connecting that count to the label.
items.lessonContent:
Measurement uncertainty concerns facts; semantic vagueness concerns how labels divide those facts.
Better instruments can solve the first without solving the second.
Exact inputs do not guarantee an exact classification rule.
Decision systems should state both the measured variable and the threshold policy.
Share this: separate the missing measurement from the missing definition in one disputed metric.

items.title: Borderline but Constrained
items.question: If a color chip is borderline red, every admissible precisification may classify it freely without regard to neighboring chips or ordinary color relations.
items.correctExplanation: False. Admissible sharpenings must preserve penumbral connections, such as clear ordering and compatibility relations among cases.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Borderline does not mean arbitrary: a precisification that calls a less red chip red while rejecting a clearly redder otherwise similar chip may violate the concept's structural constraints.
items.lessonContent:
Penumbral connections are logical and comparative relations that survive boundary uncertainty.
Admissible precisifications sharpen usage without discarding its settled structure.
Borderline cases allow alternatives, but not every imaginable assignment.
Constraints among cases can carry information even when individual labels are unsettled.
Share this: when facing a gray area, write one ordering relation that any acceptable decision must preserve.

items.title: Many Is Exact
items.question: The quantifier 'many' is logically precise whenever the total population size is known, since arithmetic then determines a unique minimum count that qualifies.
items.correctExplanation: False. Knowing the denominator constrains interpretation but does not select a unique threshold for the context-sensitive vague quantifier.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Ten may be many defections in a small committee and not many downloads in an app launch; even fixed totals do not mechanically supply the conversational standard.
items.lessonContent:
Vague quantifiers such as 'many' combine quantity with contextual expectations.
A known denominator does not uniquely determine the relevant threshold.
Purpose, comparison class, and stakes can affect what count is notable.
Replacing vague quantifiers with explicit counts improves high-stakes communication.
Share this: replace 'many' in one claim today with both a count and a denominator.

items.title: Reasonable by Rule
items.question: When a court applies the vague standard 'reasonable care,' consistency requires converting it into one universal numerical checklist that decides every future case regardless of context.
items.correctExplanation: False. Open-textured standards deliberately permit relevant circumstances to matter; consistency can come from principled analogies rather than one context-free number.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. A rigid checklist may improve predictability but discard facts the standard was designed to weigh, so like treatment requires identifying relevant similarity rather than erasing context.
items.lessonContent:
Open-textured legal terms leave room for unforeseen combinations of circumstances.
Rules maximize advance precision, while standards preserve contextual judgment.
Consistency can mean applying stable reasons to relevantly similar cases.
Sharpening a standard always trades flexibility for predictability.
Share this: identify one circumstance an apparently simple workplace rule should still allow decision-makers to weigh.

items.title: The Paired Threshold
items.question: If Ana is clearly taller than Bo and Bo is definitely tall, then any admissible interpretation of 'tall' that makes Bo tall must also make Ana tall.
items.correctExplanation: True. A height-based sharpening that accepts Bo but rejects the clearly taller Ana would violate the predicate's upward ordering.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Vagueness permits movement of the threshold, not reversal of the underlying scale; accepting a lower case commits the interpretation to accepting clearer higher cases.
items.lessonContent:
Vague predicates often preserve monotonic relations along an underlying scale.
Moving a threshold changes borderline verdicts without licensing arbitrary reversals.
Comparative facts constrain admissible categorical classifications.
Order constraints are useful when exact cutoff placement remains disputed.
Share this: in one threshold debate, state which cases must move together because of their ordering.

items.title: One Premise Must Bend
items.question: Given a clearly positive start, a clearly negative endpoint, and an apparently exceptionless rule that adjacent cases keep the same label, a consistent resolution of a finite sorites must reject or revise at least one of those commitments.
items.correctExplanation: True. Together the three commitments entail incompatible endpoint classifications, so no consistent theory can retain all of them unchanged.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Chaining the adjacent-case rule carries the starting label to the endpoint; if the endpoint has the opposite clear status, logic forces a revision somewhere in the package.
items.lessonContent:
Paradox resolution begins by displaying the smallest inconsistent set of commitments.
Rejecting an inference differs from rejecting one of its premises.
Sorites theories distribute the cost among endpoint certainty, tolerance, and classical logic.
No resolution is cost-free when individually plausible claims conflict collectively.
Share this: write three jointly conflicting claims from one dispute and mark which you would revise.

items.title: The Forced Border
items.question: A hospital must assign every temperature reading to 'fever' or 'no fever' for triage. The need for a binary action guarantees that the medical condition itself has no borderline cases.
items.correctExplanation: False. Decisions may require sharp rules even when the underlying condition, evidence, or language remains graded and borderline.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. A protocol can impose a cutoff to coordinate action; that practical necessity does not transform a continuous biological state into a naturally binary one.
items.lessonContent:
Decision boundaries and descriptive boundaries serve different roles.
Institutions often need crisp actions despite continuous evidence.
A threshold can optimize costs and benefits without defining the underlying phenomenon's essence.
Disagreement about classification need not prevent a transparent action policy.
Share this: distinguish the action cutoff from the descriptive label in one health or safety rule.

items.title: Conjunction Pressure
items.question: Suppose each of 1,000 adjacent shade pairs is judged indistinguishable in color. It can still be rational to reject the conjunction 'all 1,000 pairs have exactly the same color status' while finding no particular pair confidently rejectable.
items.correctExplanation: True. One may know that at least one tolerance step fails without possessing enough information to identify which borderline step fails.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Confidence in each local premise separately does not force confidence in their huge conjunction; accumulated risk can undermine the package without selecting a culprit.
items.lessonContent:
Many individually plausible claims can form an implausible conjunction.
Knowing that some member fails does not require knowing which member fails.
Sorites chains magnify small uncertainty across repeated tolerance steps.
Conjunction risk matters in long audits, forecasts, and reliability chains.
Share this: estimate how repeated small failure risks affect one long process you use.

items.title: Kind or Degree
items.question: Because the transition from simmering to boiling is gradual in ordinary observation, water can never undergo a scientifically meaningful phase transition at a determinate condition.
items.correctExplanation: False. Vagueness in an everyday predicate or noisy observation does not rule out a precise theoretical transition under specified pressure and equilibrium conditions.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Ordinary 'boiling' may be used loosely, but thermodynamic models can define phase boundaries precisely once relevant variables and idealizations are fixed.
items.lessonContent:
Vague observation terms and precise scientific constructs can describe related phenomena differently.
Theory may sharpen a concept by fixing variables, conditions, and measurement procedures.
An everyday borderline does not prove that every improved model must share it.
Equally, scientific precision should not be projected back into every casual use.
Share this: ask whether one everyday term has a stricter technical counterpart in a field you know.

items.title: Sharper Than Speech
items.question: If two competent speakers place the cutoff for 'nearby' at different distances but agree on all clear cases, their disagreement alone proves that one speaker misunderstands the word.
items.correctExplanation: False. Competent use can leave latitude in borderline cases while remaining stable on paradigms and practical contrasts.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Shared command of a vague term need not include one hidden numerical boundary; variation near the edge can coexist with agreement on central use.
items.lessonContent:
Linguistic competence often fixes clear cases more strongly than borderline extensions.
Reasonable speakers can sharpen one vague term differently for local purposes.
Disagreement at an edge does not erase substantial shared meaning.
Communication improves when the disputed practical threshold is stated explicitly.
Share this: when 'nearby' matters today, replace it with a distance or travel time.

items.title: Identity in Fog
items.question: If it is indeterminate whether object a is identical to object b, then substituting b for a in every precise identity statement is automatically safe, because indeterminacy behaves exactly like equality.
items.correctExplanation: False. Indeterminate identity does not license the full substitutivity guaranteed by determinate identity; treating the two alike assumes what is disputed.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Leibniz-style substitution follows from identity, but 'it is indeterminate whether a equals b' does not assert identity and therefore cannot support unrestricted replacement.
items.lessonContent:
Identity licenses substituting one name for another in extensional contexts.
Uncertainty or indeterminacy about identity is not itself an identity relation.
Vague-object debates test whether indeterminacy belongs to the world, language, or knowledge.
Do not import the consequences of a relation before establishing that the relation holds.
Share this: spot one argument today that treats 'possibly the same' as 'the same'.

items.title: Purpose Moves Borders
items.question: The same 20-minute walk may be 'near' when choosing a restaurant and 'not near' when carrying an injured person, without changing the route or committing a contradiction.
items.correctExplanation: True. Practical stakes and purpose can shift the operative standard while the measured distance remains fixed.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The contexts ask different questions of 'near': acceptable dining effort versus safe transport effort, so the threshold changes with the decision problem.
items.lessonContent:
Practical interests can help determine thresholds for context-sensitive predicates.
Stable physical facts may support different labels under different tasks.
Making the purpose explicit prevents apparent verbal disputes from masquerading as factual ones.
High stakes often demand stricter standards than casual convenience.
Share this: state the purpose behind one use of 'safe,' 'close,' or 'enough' today.
